procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 19, 1964 of the Madras High Court in Criminal Appeals Nos. 197 and 430 of 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Krishnamurthy) was convicted by the III Presidency Magistrate under s. 4(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, though charged under s. 3(1). He appealed to the High Court. The State also appealed to the High Court against the acquittal of the appellant under s. 3(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed Krishnamurthy's appeal, but allowed the State's appeal, altering the conviction to one under s. 3(1) of the Act and enhancing his punishment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Krishnamurthy appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's order. He contended that the facts did not constitute an offense under s. 3(1) of the Act and that his present conviction should not be considered a second conviction under s. 3(1) because his previous conviction was under the Madras Suppression of Immoral Traffic Act, 1930.

issue.issue_text: Whether a single instance of a house being used for prostitution, coupled with surrounding circumstances, is sufficient to establish that the house was being 'kept as a brothel' under Section 3(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956.

facts: Police received information that the appellant's house was being used as a brothel.
A police decoy was sent to the house with marked currency notes.
The appellant showed the decoy three girls to choose from.
The decoy selected one girl, paid the appellant Rs. 30 in marked notes, and went into a room with her.
The police raided the house, found the decoy and the girl in a dishevelled state, and recovered the marked notes from the appellant.
law: Section 3(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, makes it an offense to keep or manage a brothel.
Section 2(a) of the Act defines a 'brothel' as any place used for prostitution for the gain of another person.
application: The Court addressed the appellant's argument that a single, solitary instance of prostitution is not enough to prove a house is a 'brothel'.
The Court acknowledged that a single use might not be sufficient on its own, but stated that the conclusion depends on the specific facts and surrounding circumstances of the case.

The Court found the surrounding circumstances in this case to be decisive. These included the fact that a person could go to the house and freely ask for girls, be shown multiple girls to select from, and then engage one for prostitution.

The Court reasoned that these circumstances, taken together, lead to the clear conclusion that the place was being operated as a brothel and the appellant was 'keeping' it for his own financial gain, as he pocketed the money.

Crucially, the Court held that it is not necessary for the prosecution to prove repeated visits by customers. A single instance, when coupled with such compelling surrounding circumstances, is sufficient to establish the offense.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a single instance of a house being used for prostitution is sufficient to establish that it was being 'kept as a brothel' under the Act, provided that the surrounding circumstances (such as offering a choice of girls for a price) indicate an organized and commercial operation for gain.

issue.issue_text: Whether a prior conviction under the repealed Madras Suppression of Immoral Traffic Act can be considered a 'second conviction' for the purpose of enhanced sentencing under Section 3(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956.

facts: The appellant had a prior conviction under the Madras Suppression of Immoral Traffic Act, 1930 (the Madras Act).
The appellant was subsequently convicted for an offence under the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956 (the Act).
law: Section 25(1) of the 1956 Act repealed the corresponding provisions of the Madras Act.
Section 25(2) of the 1956 Act contains a 'deeming provision' which states that a conviction under the repealed Madras Act would be deemed to be a conviction under the new 1956 Act.
application: The Court applied the deeming provision in Section 25(2) of the 1956 Act.
According to this provision, the appellant's previous conviction under the Madras Act must be legally treated as if it were a conviction under the new 1956 Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court concluded that because the prior conviction under the Madras Act was 'deemed' to be a conviction under the 1956 Act, the appellant's current conviction was correctly considered a 'second conviction'. Therefore, he was liable for the enhanced punishment prescribed under Section 3(1) of the 1956 Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a single instance of a house being used for prostitution, coupled with surrounding circumstances, is sufficient to establish that the house was being 'kept as a brothel' under Section 3(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956.
appellant_arguments: The facts of the case, which involved a single police-led trap, were not sufficient to establish the offence of 'keeping a brothel' under Section 3(1) of the Act.
respondent_arguments: The facts were sufficient to prove the house was a brothel. The police had prior information, a decoy was shown three different girls, he paid the appellant marked currency notes for one of the girls, and the decoy and the girl were found in a dishevelled state, with the marked money recovered from the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a prior conviction under the repealed Madras Suppression of Immoral Traffic Act can be considered a 'second conviction' for the purpose of enhanced sentencing under Section 3(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956.
appellant_arguments: The prior conviction was under the Madras Suppression of Immoral Traffic Act, 1930, not the current 1956 Act, and therefore the present conviction cannot be considered a 'second conviction' for enhanced punishment under Section 3(1) of the 1956 Act.
respondent_arguments: Under Section 25 of the 1956 Act, the corresponding Madras Act was repealed, and any conviction under the repealed Act is 'deemed' to be a conviction under the new Act. Therefore, the prior conviction counts as the first conviction, making the current one a 'second conviction' liable for enhanced punishment.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A single instance of a place being used for prostitution, when coupled with surrounding circumstances, is sufficient to establish that the place was being kept as a brothel; evidence of repeated visits is not necessary. Additionally, a conviction under a repealed state act is deemed to be a conviction under a new, superseding act if the new act contains a savings clause to that effect, making a subsequent offense a second conviction for the purpose of sentencing.
obiter: It can be presumed that girls offered for the purpose of prostitution would also obtain monetary gain out of the amount paid.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The facts found, including a single police-led trap coupled with surrounding circumstances, were sufficient to justify the conclusion that the appellant was keeping a brothel. Furthermore, the appellant's prior conviction under the repealed Madras Act is deemed to be a conviction under the current 1956 Act by virtue of Section 25, thus making the present conviction a second conviction and warranting an enhanced punishment.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if a place is 'kept as a brothel', the court assesses if a single instance of use for prostitution, when coupled with surrounding circumstances, is sufficient to establish the character of the place and the keeper's role. It is not necessary that there should be evidence of repeated visits.

Under Section 25(2) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956, any action taken under a repealed corresponding State Act, such as a conviction, is 'deemed to have been done or taken under the provisions of this Act as if the said provisions were in force when such thing was done or such action was taken'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that a single instance of prostitution was insufficient to prove the house was a brothel failed because the court held that a single instance combined with the surrounding circumstances—such as prior information, a person freely asking for girls, being shown girls to select from, and engaging one for prostitution—is sufficient to draw the conclusion that the place was being used as a brothel.

The appellant's contention that his prior conviction under the repealed Madras Act could not be considered a 'second conviction' was rejected. The court found that Section 25(2) of the 1956 Act explicitly creates a legal fiction where the conviction under the repealed Madras Act is 'deemed to be conviction under s. 3(1) of the Act', making the current conviction a second one for the purpose of enhanced sentencing.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the facts justified the conviction for keeping a brothel. The court agreed, stating, 'The conclusion to be derived from these circumstances about the place and the person 'keeping it' can be nothing else than that the place was being used as a brothel and the person in charge was so keeping it.'

The respondent's interpretation of Section 25 of the 1956 Act was accepted by the court. The court reasoned that 'By virtue of sub-s. (2), the conviction of the appellant under s. 5(1) of the Madras Act would be deemed to be conviction under s. 3(1) of the Act... It follows that the present conviction of the appellant will have to be taken as a second conviction, within the meaning of the expression in sub-s. (!) of s. 3 of the Act.'
